flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
Sure. Okay. I recently, I had a child that I worked with a family that had two or three children, one set of twins and an older sibling. And I was always with them. And there was a lot of, they're very close in age. So there was a lot of moments where space wasn't, or, you know, personal space wasn't understood, just because you're always around the same, or your family, and don't know how to speak up in a way that, or understand that you might need personal space or be able to make your own decisions apart from, you know, being influenced by your other sibling, you know, things of that nature. I had a lot of meltdowns happening with, I guess, comments. I had a lot of competition that would, you know, you would view healthy in general, but just wanting to win all the time at anything. It could be just riding the bike to the nearest, you know, intersection, things like that. Just making things competitive in a way that could be healthy, but sometimes it's not as important. But a lot of meltdowns, you first, you know, assess the feelings and make sure that the child, both of them, felt loved. And their, you know, their feelings around whatever they were feeling, acknowledge them, make sure that they feel seen and understood, but then pivot and find a way to not, or allow our feelings to be, but not, you know, allow them to control us in a way that we don't, we no longer are making healthy choices. We're doing things that aren't acceptable. A lot of communication happens and a lot of just eye-to-eye getting down on their level and making sure that they know that, you know, I'm willing to hear them, but just directing them in a way that they understand what is acceptable and what isn't in healthy relationships and just being human, I guess. So a lot of that has happened, especially in the age that I work with, you know, the twos and threes. There's always a lot of feelings that don't know how to be articulated just yet. And I mean, even as an adult, sometimes I struggle with knowing exactly how to relay what I'm feeling to someone without reacting in a way. It's taken a lot of work. So, I mean, they've just been born, so they need a little bit of direction and just emotions. So a lot of times it's just communicate, communicate, and just try to just make sure they're heard and be direct in a way that is healthy. They can.
